verdict.summary: GE Vernova is the broadest picks-and-shovels beneficiary of global electrification in the batch, with operating evidence across gas turbines, grid equipment and wind rather than a single AI contract. Q2 2026 orders rose 88% organically to $24.2 billion, revenue increased 22% to $11.1 billion, and backlog expanded $13 billion sequentially to $176 billion. GAAP net income was $0.6 billion at a 5.8% margin; non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA reached $1.2 billion at 11.3%, up 340 basis points organically. Free cash flow of $5.1 billion and $13.1 billion cash support execution and capital returns. AI is a transmission channel, not the whole thesis: data-center orders exceeded $5 billion year to date, more than twice full-year 2025. The problem is valuation and delivery duration. Point-in-time EV/EBITDA is about 62.7x and EV/revenue roughly 6.0x, while backlog carries inflation, warranty and supply-chain risk. The February $2.6 billion notes were straight debt, not equity. The B grade is defensible; trade status remains watch above $948.59.

business.overview:
GE Vernova sells gas-power equipment and services, grid hardware and software, and wind turbines and services. Revenue is driven by equipment deliveries, long-cycle backlog conversion, service outages, pricing, manufacturing productivity and project execution across three distinct businesses.

The AI transmission channel is upstream power infrastructure: datacenter load requires new gas generation, transformers, switchgear and grid modernization. More than $5B of year-to-date data-center orders therefore enters Power and Electrification backlogs directly, while service agreements monetize the installed base for years.

The model breaks if turbine slots or grid equipment are delivered late, input inflation outruns contract pricing, wind losses persist, warranties rise or customers defer projects. A $176B backlog improves visibility but also locks in execution obligations across currencies and supply chains. At more than 60x trailing EV/EBITDA, the equity requires both backlog conversion and margin expansion. Investors should therefore monitor segment margin, working-capital release, cancellation behavior and service attachment as backlog converts, rather than treating every booked dollar as equally profitable.
business.moat: GE Vernova combines a massive installed turbine base, scarce gas-turbine manufacturing slots, long-lived service relationships and grid equipment breadth. Switching costs and qualification cycles are real, but the moat is strongest in Power and Electrification and weaker where wind projects remain operationally difficult.

capitalStructure.shareHistory: GE Vernova's June filing reports $12.720B unrestricted cash and cash equivalents plus $0.400B restricted cash, for $13.120B total cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, versus about $3.7B debt. Period-end common shares were approximately 266.3M, while Q2 diluted weighted-average shares were 270M after common-stock equivalents; that 3.7M EPS bridge is observable dilution exposure, not proof of an offering, and a point-in-time fully diluted count is unavailable. The February 3, 2026 424B5 documents $2.6B of straight senior notes, not equity. Related 424B3 and S-3ASR filings provide registration capacity but do not prove common shares were sold.

filings.finding: The June Form 10-Q reports $11.1B Q2 revenue, segment execution, cash, debt and working-capital movements, supporting current profitability and backlog-conversion analysis. This classification controls the editorial conclusion.
The 2025 Form 10-K establishes GE Vernova's annual segment, warranty, supply-chain, controls and capital baseline; it predates the Q2 order surge and raised 2026 outlook.
The August Form 8-K reports a later material company event disclosed on that date; it should not be used to source July Q2 KPIs or reclassify prior debt as equity.
The February 424B5 documents $2.6B of senior notes as straight debt securities with interest and repayment obligations; it does not evidence any common-stock issuance or dilution.
The February 424B3 provides base prospectus terms for registered securities; it does not by itself establish a completed common offering, ATM sale or financing proceeds.

The January S-3ASR establishes automatic shelf capacity across eligible securities; only a later transaction-specific prospectus can establish whether debt or equity was actually sold. This classification controls the editorial conclusion.

contrarianRisks: The $2.6B February note offering was straight senior debt, not common-equity issuance.
